tool.name: Hugging Face Transformers
tool.tagline: Pretrained transformer models for text, vision and audio, plus training and generation
tool.description: Transformers is Hugging Face's library of pretrained model architectures (BERT, Llama, Qwen, Whisper, ViT and hundreds more) with a uniform API to download, run, fine-tune and share them. It covers quick inference with pipelines, tokenization, the Trainer training loop, text generation for LLMs, and integrations for LoRA fine-tuning and quantization. It is the default entry point to open-weight models on the Hugging Face Hub.

glossary.def: The neural-network design behind modern language models, built from attention layers that let every token weigh every other token. Transformers, capitalised, is also Hugging Face's library for these models.
Hugging Face's website where people publish and download pretrained models and datasets, each in its own named repository.

A saved set of model files (its settings, learned weights and usually its tokenizer) that you load by name, such as google-bert/bert-base-uncased, or from a folder. Trainer also saves checkpoints during a run so training can resume.
The numbers a tokenizer turns text into (called input_ids in code): each is one token's position in the model's vocabulary. They are what the model actually reads.

The list of numbers (a vector) that a transformer layer produces for each token, describing that token in the context of the whole input. The last layer's hidden states are what the task-specific part of the model reads.
A token with a fixed job rather than a piece of text, such as marking where the input starts or ends, separating two sentences, or filling space.
The special filler token added to shorter texts so every text in a batch has the same length. The attention mask tells the model to ignore it.
A list of 1s and 0s that goes with the token IDs: 1 marks a real token, 0 marks filler (padding) that the model should ignore.
A token that is only part of a word, such as 'token' + '##ization'. Splitting rare words into pieces lets a fixed vocabulary spell out any text.
The README page of a model on the Hub: what it's for, what data it learned from, its license and its known limitations.
The standard file format for model weights. It loads quickly and, unlike files made with Python's pickle, can't contain code that runs when the file is opened.
A model on the Hub that you can download only after logging in and accepting its license on its web page.
One specific saved version of a Hub repo, named by a label or an ID. Loading a fixed revision guarantees you get the same files every time, even if the owner updates the repo.
A Transformers class such as AutoModel or AutoTokenizer that reads a checkpoint's settings and picks the matching model or tokenizer class for you.
Sorting text into categories that you name only when you ask, with no training examples for those categories.
Named-entity recognition: finding the names of people, places, organisations and similar things in a text and labelling each one.
Natural language inference: judging whether one sentence follows from, contradicts or is unrelated to another. Zero-shot classification reuses models trained for it.
A standard way to store tables of data, column by column, in memory and in files. The datasets library keeps data in Arrow files so it can read just the parts it needs.
A model that writes text by predicting each next token from the tokens before it, never looking ahead. GPT, Llama and Qwen are causal language models.
The special token a model outputs to say its text is finished; generation stops when it appears.
The rule for picking each next token from the model's probabilities while generating, such as always taking the likeliest one (greedy) or drawing one at random (sampling).
Generating by always taking the single most likely next token. The same prompt always gives the same output.
Generating by drawing each next token at random, weighted by the model's probabilities, so the same prompt can give different outputs.
A sampling setting that reshapes the next-token probabilities: below 1 makes likely tokens even likelier (safer, more predictable text), above 1 evens them out (more varied text).
A sampling setting: draw only from the most likely tokens that together reach probability p (such as 0.9), cutting off the long tail of unlikely ones. Also called nucleus sampling.
A sampling setting: draw only from the k most likely next tokens.
Generation that follows several candidate continuations at once and keeps the one with the best overall score. It suits tasks with one right answer, such as translation.
An LLM fine-tuned on example conversations so that it answers requests and follows instructions instead of just continuing the text.
A small template shipped with a chat model's tokenizer that turns a list of messages into the exact text format, special tokens included, that the model was trained on.
A function that takes a list of examples and stacks them into one batch of tensors, padding each batch only as much as it needs.
Padding each batch only up to its own longest example, instead of padding every example to one fixed maximum length.
A model such as BERT trained to fill in hidden words in a sentence using the words on both sides. Good for understanding text, not for writing it.
Transformers' ready-made training loop: give it a model, data and settings, and it handles batches, optimizer steps, evaluation, saving and multiple GPUs.
A score from 0 to 1 that balances how many predicted positives were right with how many real positives were found. Macro F1 averages it over the classes, so rare classes count as much as common ones.
Low-Rank Adaptation: fine-tuning that freezes a model's weights and trains small add-on matrices (adapters) for some of its layers, often well under 1% of its parameters.
A small set of extra trained weights added on top of a frozen pretrained model. It can be saved, shared and swapped separately from the model.
Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning: Hugging Face's library for fine-tuning a small number of extra weights, such as LoRA adapters, instead of the whole model.
A library that stores model weights in 8 or 4 bits as they are loaded. Transformers uses it for quantized loading and for QLoRA.
A 4-bit number format designed for neural-network weights, which mostly cluster near zero in a bell-curve shape. The usual choice for QLoRA.
A method that quantizes a model ahead of time, using a small sample of text to keep accuracy. GPTQ checkpoints are published already quantized.
Activation-aware weight quantization: a method that quantizes a model to 4 bits ahead of time while protecting the weights that matter most. AWQ checkpoints are published already quantized.
LoRA fine-tuning on top of a model loaded in 4-bit form, so that large models can be fine-tuned on a single GPU.
Hugging Face's library for training LLMs on instructions and on human feedback, with ready-made trainers such as SFTTrainer.
During generation, the stored keys and values (intermediate results of every attention layer) for all tokens so far, so each new token needs only its own calculation.
The first step of generation: the whole prompt goes through the model at once and fills the KV cache. After it, each step adds one token.
The code that actually computes attention inside a model, such as sdpa, FlashAttention or eager. Transformers lets you swap it without changing the model.
Splitting each layer's weight matrices across several GPUs, so that all of them work on every layer at the same time.
Hugging Face's library that places models on devices and runs training on one or many GPUs. Trainer and device_map="auto" use it behind the scenes.
Microsoft's library for training very large models across many GPUs, best known for its ZeRO memory-saving stages.
Byte-pair encoding: building a tokenizer's vocabulary by repeatedly merging the most frequent pair of neighbouring symbols into a new token. Used by GPT, Llama and Qwen.
BERT's way of splitting words into pieces, similar to BPE but choosing merges by how much they help; it marks a piece that continues a word with ##.
A way of building a tokenizer vocabulary that starts from a very large list of pieces and removes the least useful ones. Used by T5, through SentencePiece.
A tokenizer library from Google that works on raw text, spaces included, and can build BPE or Unigram vocabularies.
Rotary position embedding: how most modern LLMs tell the model where each token sits in the text, by rotating its vectors by an angle that depends on the position.

concepts.name: Transformer models, tokens and the Hub
concepts.summary: What the Transformers library is for: pretrained transformer models shared on the Hub, and the tokens they read instead of letters.
concepts.why: Every other lesson uses these words; knowing them makes the rest of the course easy to follow.
concepts.body:
Earlier you saw that a model is a formula with millions of learned weights, and that training those weights takes lots of data and GPU time. Training a big model from nothing can cost a fortune, but you rarely have to: companies and researchers publish their trained models for anyone to download.

**Hugging Face** is the company behind the main website for sharing them, the **Hub**. Its Python library **Transformers** downloads and runs those models in a few lines of code.

Most of these models share one neural-network design, the **transformer**. Its key layer is **attention**: while working on one word, the model weighs every other word in the input by how relevant it is. In "the bank of the river", attention is what lets the model read "bank" as a riverbank rather than a place for money.

A model can't read letters, only numbers. So text is first cut into **tokens**: short, common chunks of text, sometimes a whole word ("the") and sometimes part of one ("token" + "ization"). The model has a fixed list of every token it knows, its **vocabulary**, and each token is replaced by its position in that list. Those numbers are the **token IDs** (called `input_ids` in code).

The software that does this cutting and numbering is a **tokenizer**. Every model comes with its own, because it learned with that exact vocabulary.

A model published on the Hub is called a **checkpoint**: a named set of files, such as `google-bert/bert-base-uncased`, holding the model's settings, its learned weights and its tokenizer. Download one and you have a pretrained model, ready to use as it is or to train a little more on your own examples. That extra training is called **fine-tuning**.

The best-known transformers are **large language models** (LLMs) such as Llama or Qwen. They are trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next token, over and over, which is how chatbots write their answers. The same library also runs smaller transformers that sort or tag text, and models for images and audio.
concepts.code:
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

# downloads only the tokenizer files of a checkpoint from the Hub
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("google-bert/bert-base-uncased")

print(tok.tokenize("Hello world!"))
# ['hello', 'world', '!']
print(tok("Hello world!")["input_ids"])
# [101, 7592, 2088, 999, 102]   101 and 102 mark the start and end
print(tok.tokenize("tokenization"))
# ['token', '##ization']        a rarer word becomes two pieces
print(len(tok))
# 30522                         tokens in this model's vocabulary
takeaways: Transformers downloads and runs pretrained models shared on the Hugging Face Hub
Text is cut into tokens, and each token becomes an ID from the model's vocabulary
A checkpoint is a named model on the Hub: settings, weights and tokenizer
Fine-tuning is training a pretrained model a little more on your own data
pitfalls: Loading the model from one checkpoint and the tokenizer from another: the token IDs then point at the wrong vocabulary and the output is nonsense.

quiz.q: Why does every checkpoint come with its own tokenizer?
options: Tokenizers are too large to share between models
The model learned with one exact vocabulary, so text must be cut and numbered exactly the same way
The Hub requires one tokenizer per upload
quiz.explain: A token ID only means something in the vocabulary the model was trained with; another tokenizer would give it the wrong numbers.

quiz.q: What is fine-tuning?
options: Training a pretrained model a little more on your own examples
Downloading a model from the Hub
quiz.explain: Fine-tuning starts from the learned weights of a pretrained model and adjusts them for your task.

concepts.name: Pipelines: inference in three lines
concepts.summary: Run a pretrained model on raw text, images or audio with pipeline(), which handles the steps before and after the model for you.
concepts.why: Pipelines are the fastest way to try a model or ship a simple inference feature.
concepts.body:
Using a model takes three steps: turn your raw input into numbers, run the model, and turn the numbers it outputs back into something readable. A **pipeline** does all three in a single call:

```python
clf = pipeline("text-classification", model="distilbert/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english")
```

The first argument names the **task**, the kind of job you want done: here, sorting text into categories. `model=` names the checkpoint to download from the Hub. Always pass it: without it the pipeline picks a default model for the task, which can change between library versions, and it prints a warning.

Behind the scenes the pipeline runs the tokenizer on your text, feeds the token IDs through the model, and turns the model's logits into a label plus a score, how confident the model is, from 0 to 1.

Useful arguments:

- `device=0` runs on the first GPU, `device="cpu"` on the CPU, and `device_map="auto"` spreads a model too big for one GPU over the GPUs and memory you have.
- `dtype="auto"` (the default in version 5) loads the weights in the number format they were saved in; `torch.bfloat16` forces a 2-byte format that halves memory.
- Pass a **list** of inputs and `batch_size=` to handle many items per step, much faster on a GPU than one at a time.

Text tasks take a string or a list of strings. Image and audio tasks also take a file path or a web address (a URL). The model's files are downloaded once and kept in a local **cache**, a folder of saved downloads (`~/.cache/huggingface/hub`), so later runs start without downloading again.

Pipelines trade control for convenience. When you need your own batching, the model's inner numbers, or training, use the tokenizer and model classes directly, as the next lessons show. Version 5 removed a few older tasks such as `summarization` and `translation`; ask an LLM through `text-generation` instead.
concepts.code:
from transformers import pipeline

clf = pipeline(
    "text-classification",
    model="distilbert/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english",
)
print(clf("I love this library!"))
# [{'label': 'POSITIVE', 'score': 0.999...}]

reviews = ["Terrible support.", "Works great, fast shipping."]
for r in clf(reviews, batch_size=2):
    print(r["label"], round(r["score"], 3))
# NEGATIVE 0.999...
# POSITIVE 0.999...

asr = pipeline("automatic-speech-recognition", model="openai/whisper-tiny")
# asr("meeting.wav") -> {'text': ' Hello everyone, ...'}
takeaways: `pipeline(task, model=...)` = prepare the input + run the model + make the output readable
Always name the checkpoint with `model=` instead of relying on the task default
Pass lists with `batch_size` for speed; use `device`/`device_map` for GPUs
pitfalls: Calling a pipeline on one string at a time inside a loop on a GPU, which leaves most of the GPU idle.

quiz.q: Why should you pass model= when creating a pipeline?
options: The default model for a task may change between versions, so your results could change too
It is required to use a GPU
It stops downloads from the Hub
quiz.explain: Without model= the task's default is used, which can change and is only meant for quick experiments.

concepts.name: The Hub, checkpoints and caching
concepts.summary: Find models on the Hugging Face Hub, fix the version you load, understand the download cache and safetensors, and treat a repo's own code with care.
concepts.why: Every from_pretrained call goes through the Hub; knowing how it finds files keeps your model from changing under you and avoids security mistakes.
concepts.body:
Every checkpoint lives on the Hub in its own **repository**, or repo: a folder of files whose every change is recorded by version control, so older versions stay available. A repo is named `owner/name`, for example `Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct`.

A typical model repo contains:

- `config.json`: the model's settings, such as how many layers it has.
- `model.safetensors`: the learned weights. A big model splits them into several files, called **shards**, plus an index file listing them.
- the tokenizer's files, and `generation_config.json` with default settings for writing text.
- a **model card** (`README.md`): what the model is for, what data it learned from, its license and its known limits.

`from_pretrained("owner/name")` downloads these files into a local cache folder (`~/.cache/huggingface/hub`) and reuses them on later runs. To move that folder, set `HF_HOME`, an **environment variable**: a named setting your system hands to every program it starts.

Useful options:

- `revision="..."` loads one specific saved version of the repo, a **revision**, instead of the latest. Fix it for anything real users rely on, so the owner updating the repo can't silently change your model.
- `token=`, or running `hf auth login` once, gives access to private repos and to **gated** ones, where you must first accept the license on the model's web page.
- `HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1` makes loading use only the cache, for machines without internet.
- A path to a folder on your own disk works anywhere a repo name does.

**safetensors** is the standard file format for weights. It loads fast and, unlike older `.bin` files made with **pickle** (Python's tool for saving any object to a file), it can't hide code that runs when you open it.

`trust_remote_code=True` lets a repo run its own Python code on your machine to build the model. Only turn it on for repos you trust, at a fixed revision. The popular model designs are built into Transformers and need no such code.

Read the license on the model card before using a model in a product: free to download doesn't always mean free to use commercially.
concepts.code:
from huggingface_hub import list_repo_files, snapshot_download
from transformers import AutoConfig

repo = "Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct"
print(list_repo_files(repo)[:5])
# ['.gitattributes', 'LICENSE', 'README.md', 'config.json', ...]

config = AutoConfig.from_pretrained(repo)      # downloads only config.json
print(config.model_type, config.num_hidden_layers)   # qwen2 24

# load a fixed version of the repo (a version name or ID; "main" is the latest)
config = AutoConfig.from_pretrained(repo, revision="main")

# download a whole repo once, then load from the local folder
path = snapshot_download(repo, allow_patterns=["*.json", "*.safetensors"])
print(path)   # ~/.cache/huggingface/hub/models--Qwen--Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct/...
takeaways: A checkpoint is a Hub repo with a config, safetensors weights and tokenizer files
Fix `revision` for anything users rely on; downloads are cached under HF_HOME
Only use `trust_remote_code=True` for repos you trust, at a fixed revision
pitfalls: Loading a model with trust_remote_code=True from an unknown repo, which runs whatever code its author wrote on your machine.

quiz.q: What does trust_remote_code=True allow?
options: Running Python code shipped in the model's repo to build the model
quiz.explain: It lets code from the repo run on your machine, which is why you should only use it with sources you trust.

concepts.name: Tokenizers: text to input IDs
concepts.summary: Convert text into token IDs and attention masks with AutoTokenizer, including padding, truncation and decoding.
concepts.why: Models only see integers; the wrong tokenizer or missing padding silently ruins results.
concepts.body:
A tokenizer turns text into the token IDs a model reads, and back. Always load the one that belongs to your checkpoint: `AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(repo)`. Another model's tokenizer numbers tokens differently, so the model gets nonsense, and nothing raises an error.

Calling the tokenizer on text returns a dictionary-like `BatchEncoding`:

- `input_ids`: the token IDs. They include **special tokens**, extra tokens with a fixed job such as marking where the text starts or ends: `[CLS]` and `[SEP]` for BERT, or a start token (often called BOS, "beginning of sequence") for many LLMs.
- `attention_mask`: 1 for each real token and 0 for filler (see padding below). This **attention mask** tells the model's attention layers to skip the filler.
- Some models also return `token_type_ids`, which mark which of two sentences each token came from.

A tensor needs rows of equal length, so a batch of texts of different lengths must be evened out:

- `padding=True` adds filler **pad tokens** to the shorter texts, up to the longest one in the batch; `padding="max_length"` pads up to `max_length`.
- `truncation=True` cuts texts longer than `max_length` (or the model's limit).
- `return_tensors="pt"` returns PyTorch tensors instead of Python lists.

`tokenizer.tokenize(text)` shows the token strings, and `tokenizer.decode(ids, skip_special_tokens=True)` turns IDs back into text. A rare word is split into several **subword** pieces: BERT turns `tokenization` into `token` + `##ization`, where `##` marks a piece that continues a word. That is how a fixed vocabulary of 30,000 to 150,000 entries can still spell out any text.

Transformers' tokenizers are written in Rust, a fast compiled language, so tokenizing thousands of texts takes moments.

Count in tokens, not characters. A model can read only a limited number of tokens at once, its **context window**, and online model services charge per token.
concepts.code:
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("google-bert/bert-base-uncased")

enc = tok("Hello world!")
print(enc["input_ids"])          # [101, 7592, 2088, 999, 102]
print(tok.convert_ids_to_tokens(enc["input_ids"]))
# ['[CLS]', 'hello', 'world', '!', '[SEP]']
print(tok.tokenize("tokenization"))   # ['token', '##ization']

batch = tok(["short one", "a somewhat longer sentence here"],
            padding=True, truncation=True, max_length=16, return_tensors="pt")
print(batch["input_ids"].shape)  # torch.Size([2, 7])
print(batch["attention_mask"][0])  # tensor([1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0])

print(tok.decode(batch["input_ids"][0], skip_special_tokens=True))  # short one
takeaways: Always load the tokenizer from the same checkpoint as the model
Batches need `padding` and usually `truncation`; the attention mask marks the real tokens
Use `return_tensors="pt"` to feed the model directly
pitfalls: Forgetting truncation, so a long input is longer than the model's maximum and raises an index error.

quiz.q: What is the attention_mask for?
options: It hides special tokens from the output
It marks which tokens are real and which are padding
It lists which layers use attention
quiz.explain: The mask is 1 for real tokens and 0 for padding, so attention ignores the pad positions.

concepts.name: Auto classes and task heads
concepts.summary: Load the right model and task head with AutoModel and AutoModelFor... classes and from_pretrained.
concepts.why: Auto classes let the same code load BERT, Qwen or Llama; choosing the right head decides what the model outputs.
concepts.body:
`from_pretrained` reads a checkpoint's `config.json`, builds the matching model design and loads the weights into it. **Auto classes** pick the right model class from that config for you, so the same code loads BERT, Qwen or Llama.

A model has two parts. The **backbone** is the big pretrained part: it reads the tokens and produces, for each token, a vector of numbers describing what that token means in this sentence, its **hidden state**.

The **head** is a small final layer on top that turns those vectors into the answer for one task, such as a score per category. The class name picks the head:

- `AutoModel`: the backbone alone, returning hidden states.
- `AutoModelForSequenceClassification`: adds a classification head, returning `logits`, one score per label.
- `AutoModelForTokenClassification` (a label for every token, such as marking names of people and places), `AutoModelForQuestionAnswering`, `AutoModelForCausalLM` (writing text), `AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM` (read one text, write another, as in translation), `AutoModelForImageClassification`, and more.

Loading a backbone with a **new head** is how fine-tuning starts: `AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-uncased", num_labels=3)` creates the head with random weights and prints a warning listing these newly initialised weights. That warning is expected before training, but alarming if you meant to load a classifier that was already trained.

Common loading options:

- `dtype="auto"` (the default in version 5) keeps the checkpoint's number format; `dtype=torch.bfloat16` uses half the memory of float32.
- `device_map="auto"` spreads the layers over your GPUs and the CPU, which a model too big for one GPU needs. (Hugging Face's **Accelerate** library does the placing.)
- `id2label`/`label2id` attach readable label names to the config.

The model is an ordinary `torch.nn.Module`: call `.to("cuda")` or `.eval()`, look at `.config`, or count its parameters with `model.num_parameters()`.
concepts.code:
import torch
from transformers import AutoModel, AutoModelForSequenceClassification, AutoTokenizer

name = "google-bert/bert-base-uncased"
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(name)

backbone = AutoModel.from_pretrained(name)
out = backbone(**tok("hello", return_tensors="pt"))
print(out.last_hidden_state.shape)     # torch.Size([1, 3, 768])  3 tokens x 768 numbers

clf = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(
    name, num_labels=3,
    id2label={0: "neg", 1: "neu", 2: "pos"}, label2id={"neg": 0, "neu": 1, "pos": 2},
)   # warns: Some weights ... are newly initialized: ['classifier.bias', 'classifier.weight']
print(clf.config.id2label[2])          # pos
print(f"{clf.num_parameters():,}")     # 109,484,547

half = AutoModel.from_pretrained(name, dtype=torch.bfloat16)
print(next(half.parameters()).dtype)   # torch.bfloat16
takeaways: Auto classes pick the model class from config.json
The `...For<Task>` class decides the head and what the model outputs
A 'newly initialized' warning means the head still needs training
pitfalls: Loading a base checkpoint with AutoModelForSequenceClassification and using it for predictions without fine-tuning; the head is random.

quiz.q: You load bert-base-uncased with AutoModelForSequenceClassification(num_labels=2) and immediately predict. What do you get?
options: Essentially random predictions, because the classification head is untrained
An error: the checkpoint has no classifier
The hidden states instead of logits
quiz.explain: The base checkpoint has no classifier weights, so the head is randomly initialised and must be fine-tuned.

concepts.name: Running a model by hand
concepts.summary: Tokenize, run the forward pass under inference mode, and turn logits into probabilities and labels yourself.
concepts.why: Doing by hand what a pipeline does gives you control over batching, access to hidden states and your own handling of the outputs.
concepts.body:
Running a model by hand takes four steps:

1. Tokenize a batch with `padding=True, truncation=True, return_tensors="pt"` and move the tensors to the model's device: `inputs = inputs.to(model.device)`.
2. Put the model in evaluation mode with `model.eval()`, which switches off dropout. `from_pretrained` already does this, but it matters after training.
3. Run the forward pass inside `torch.inference_mode()` (or `torch.no_grad()`), so no autograd graph is built. That saves memory and time.
4. Read the results. The output is a `ModelOutput` object with attributes such as `.logits`, `.hidden_states` (when you pass `output_hidden_states=True`) or `.loss` (when you pass `labels`).

For classification, `logits.softmax(-1)` gives probabilities and `logits.argmax(-1)` the index of the predicted class; look its name up in `model.config.id2label`.

To get one embedding for a whole sentence from an `AutoModel`, a common approach is **mean pooling**: average the last layer's hidden states over the real tokens only, using the attention mask, so the padding doesn't water the result down. Models trained specially for embeddings (the sentence-transformers checkpoints on the Hub) do this job much better than plain BERT.

Run data in batches as large as your memory allows. Sorting texts by length first puts similar lengths together, so less of each batch is padding and more of the work is real.
concepts.code:
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForSequenceClassification, AutoTokenizer

name = "distilbert/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english"
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(name)
model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(name).eval()

texts = ["What a fantastic movie", "Boring and far too long"]
inputs = tok(texts, padding=True, truncation=True, return_tensors="pt").to(model.device)

with torch.inference_mode():
    logits = model(**inputs).logits          # shape (2, 2)

probs = logits.softmax(dim=-1)
for text, p in zip(texts, probs):
    label = model.config.id2label[int(p.argmax())]
    print(f"{label:8} {p.max():.3f}  {text}")
# POSITIVE 1.000  What a fantastic movie
# NEGATIVE 1.000  Boring and far too long
takeaways: Tokenize a batch, move it to `model.device`, run under `torch.inference_mode()`
Outputs are ModelOutput objects: use `.logits`, `.hidden_states`, `.loss`
Mean pooling over real tokens turns hidden states into a sentence embedding
pitfalls: Leaving inputs on the CPU while the model is on the GPU, which raises a device mismatch error.

quiz.q: Why wrap inference in torch.inference_mode()?
options: It avoids building the autograd graph, saving memory and time
It switches the model to evaluation mode
It moves tensors to the GPU
It is required for softmax to work
quiz.explain: Gradients aren't needed for predictions, so not tracking them saves memory and work; eval() is a separate step.

concepts.name: Choosing pipeline tasks
concepts.summary: Use zero-shot classification, entity finding, fill-mask, embeddings and image or audio tasks, and tune their key options.
concepts.why: Picking the right task and options often solves a problem without any training.
concepts.body:
Beyond plain classification, pipelines cover many everyday jobs. A few, with the options worth knowing:

- `zero-shot-classification`: sorts text into categories you name only at call time, with no training examples for them. Pass `candidate_labels=[...]`; set `multi_label=True` when several labels can apply at once. It uses a model trained for **NLI**, judging whether one sentence follows from another, such as `facebook/bart-large-mnli`.
- `token-classification` (or `ner`): **named-entity recognition**, finding names of people, places and organisations. Use `aggregation_strategy="simple"` to merge word pieces into whole names like `"New York"` instead of `"New"`, `"##York"`.
- `fill-mask`: predicts a hidden word you mark with `[MASK]`; handy for probing what a model learned.
- `feature-extraction`: returns the model's **hidden states**, one vector of numbers per token describing it in context; a quick route to embeddings.
- `text-generation`: LLM text writing or chat (covered in the generation module).
- Images and audio: `image-classification`, `object-detection`, `image-text-to-text` for models that answer questions about pictures, and `automatic-speech-recognition` with Whisper, a speech-to-text model.

Each task returns its own result shape: lists of dicts with `label`/`score`, `entity_group`/`start`/`end`, `sequence`/`token_str` and so on. Read the task's section in the pipelines reference to know what to expect.

Pick a model fine-tuned for the task: the Hub's task filters list suitable checkpoints. A general model under a task pipeline will run, but its results will be meaningless.
concepts.code:
from transformers import pipeline

zs = pipeline("zero-shot-classification", model="facebook/bart-large-mnli")
res = zs("The battery dies after two hours.",
         candidate_labels=["battery", "screen", "price"])
print(res["labels"][0])          # battery

ner = pipeline("ner", model="dslim/bert-base-NER", aggregation_strategy="simple")
for ent in ner("Ada Lovelace was born in London."):
    print(ent["entity_group"], ent["word"])
# PER Ada Lovelace
# LOC London

fill = pipeline("fill-mask", model="google-bert/bert-base-uncased")
print(fill("Paris is the [MASK] of France.")[0]["token_str"])   # capital
takeaways: Zero-shot classification handles labels you choose at run time
Use `aggregation_strategy="simple"` to get whole names from NER
Choose a checkpoint fine-tuned for the task you run
pitfalls: Running NER without an aggregation strategy and then trying to glue '##' word pieces back together by hand.

quiz.q: You need to tag support tickets with categories that change every week, with no training data. Which task fits?
quiz.explain: Zero-shot classification takes the candidate labels at call time, so no retraining is needed.

concepts.name: Loading data with Datasets
concepts.summary: Load, inspect, split and transform data with Hugging Face's datasets library.
concepts.why: Transformers' training tools and most examples expect datasets.Dataset objects; map and splits are the everyday tools.
concepts.body:
Fine-tuning needs examples to learn from. Hugging Face's companion library **datasets** (`pip install datasets`) loads them from the Hub or from your own files, and the training tools later in this course expect data in its format.

A loaded dataset is a table: each row is one example, each column one field such as `text` or `label`. It is kept on disk in the **Arrow** format and memory-mapped: the program reads only the parts it needs straight from the file, so a dataset far bigger than your RAM (the computer's fast working memory) still works.

- `load_dataset("stanfordnlp/imdb")` returns a `DatasetDict` of named parts, called **splits** (`train`, `test`).
- `load_dataset("csv", data_files="reviews.csv")` (or `"json"`, `"parquet"`) loads local files.
- `Dataset.from_dict({...})` builds a small dataset straight from a Python dict.

`ds[0]` returns one row as a dict. `ds.column_names` and `ds.num_rows` describe the table, and `ds.features` gives each column's type, such as `ClassLabel`, which stores label numbers together with their names.

The main tool is `ds.map(fn, batched=True)`. Your function `fn` receives a batch of rows as a dict of lists, one list per column, and returns new or changed columns. The results are saved in a cache on disk, a store of finished work, so running the script again skips steps already done.

Other everyday methods:

- `filter(fn)`, `select(range(1000))` for a quick subset, `shuffle(seed=42)`.
- `train_test_split(test_size=0.1, seed=42)` to set aside a validation split.
- `remove_columns`, `rename_column`, `cast_column` (change a column's type).
- `set_format("torch")` or `with_format("torch")` to get tensors back.

For data too large to download, `load_dataset(..., streaming=True)` returns an `IterableDataset` that reads examples one by one as you loop over it.
concepts.code:
from datasets import Dataset

ds = Dataset.from_dict({
    "text": ["great film", "awful plot", "loved it", "meh", "superb cast", "boring"],
    "label": [1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0],
})
print(ds)               # Dataset({features: ['text', 'label'], num_rows: 6})
print(ds[0])            # {'text': 'great film', 'label': 1}

def add_length(batch):  # batched: gets lists, returns new columns
    return {"n_words": [len(t.split()) for t in batch["text"]]}

ds = ds.map(add_length, batched=True)
short = ds.filter(lambda ex: ex["n_words"] == 1)
print(list(short["text"]))  # ['meh', 'boring']

splits = ds.train_test_split(test_size=0.33, seed=42)
print(splits["train"].num_rows, splits["test"].num_rows)   # 4 2
# from datasets import load_dataset; imdb = load_dataset("stanfordnlp/imdb")
takeaways: `load_dataset` returns splits stored on disk and read only as needed
`map(fn, batched=True)` is the main transformation, and its results are cached
Use `train_test_split`, `select` and `filter` to shape data
pitfalls: Using batched=True but writing fn as if it received a single example, so it operates on lists by mistake.

quiz.q: With ds.map(fn, batched=True), what does fn receive?
options: One example as a dict of single values
A dict mapping each column to a list of values for a batch of rows
quiz.explain: Batched map passes a dict of column lists and expects lists back, which is much faster than one call per row.

concepts.name: Generating text with causal LMs
concepts.summary: Load an LLM with AutoModelForCausalLM and generate text from a prompt with model.generate.
concepts.why: Text generation is the core of chatbots, assistants and most modern LLM use.
concepts.body:
An LLM writes one token at a time. Given the tokens so far, it gives every token in its vocabulary a score for how likely it is to come next. A model that works this way, only ever looking back at earlier tokens, is called a **causal language model**.

To generate, the library picks a token, appends it, and repeats. It stops when the model outputs its special end token, the **EOS token** ("end of sequence"), or when a length limit is reached.

Load a model with:

```python
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(repo, dtype="auto", device_map="auto")
```

Then tokenize a **prompt**, the text you want the model to continue, call `model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=50)`, and decode the result. Key points:

- **Always set `max_new_tokens`.** The default length is short (often 20 tokens) and cuts the output off without any warning.
- `generate` returns the prompt plus the new tokens. Slice the prompt off (`out[:, inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]:]`) before decoding if you only want the new text.
- By default the model takes the single most likely token every time, **greedy decoding**, unless the checkpoint's `generation_config.json` turns on **sampling**, a random pick weighted by the scores. Many models tuned for chat ship with sampling on, so the same prompt can give different answers.
- To generate for several prompts at once, set `tok.padding_side = "left"`: the filler goes before the shorter prompts, so every prompt ends at the same position, right where new text starts. Also make sure a pad token exists (`tok.pad_token = tok.eos_token` if it's missing).

Small models like `HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-135M-Instruct` or `Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct` run on a laptop CPU and are ideal for learning. The `text-generation` pipeline wraps all of this, including chat formatting, when you just need outputs.
concepts.code:
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

repo = "HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-135M"
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(repo)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(repo, dtype="auto")

inputs = tok("The three primary colors are", return_tensors="pt").to(model.device)
out = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=20, do_sample=False)

new_tokens = out[0, inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]:]   # drop the prompt
print(tok.decode(new_tokens, skip_special_tokens=True))
# e.g. " red, yellow and blue. ..."

# batched prompts need left padding for decoder-only models
tok.padding_side = "left"
if tok.pad_token is None:
    tok.pad_token = tok.eos_token
batch = tok(["Hello, my name is", "Python is"], return_tensors="pt", padding=True)
outs = model.generate(**batch, max_new_tokens=10)
print(len(tok.batch_decode(outs, skip_special_tokens=True)))   # 2
takeaways: `AutoModelForCausalLM` + `generate` writes text one token at a time
Always set `max_new_tokens`, and cut the prompt off before decoding
Use left padding and a pad token when generating for several prompts at once
pitfalls: Padding on the right when generating for several prompts at once, which makes the model continue after the filler and produce junk.

quiz.q: Generating for several prompts at once gives garbage for the shorter prompts only. What is the likely cause?
options: The tokenizer pads on the right instead of the left
quiz.explain: A causal model continues from the last position, so shorter prompts must be padded on the left to end where new text begins.

concepts.name: Preprocessing and data collators
concepts.summary: Tokenize a dataset with map and let a data collator pad each batch only as much as it needs.
concepts.why: Correct, efficient batching is half the work of fine-tuning and a common source of shape errors.
concepts.body:
Before training, turn the text columns into model inputs. The usual way is a batched `map` with the tokenizer:

```python
def tokenize(batch):
    return tok(batch["text"], truncation=True, max_length=256)
ds = ds.map(tokenize, batched=True, remove_columns=["text"])
```

Notice there is **no padding** here. Padding every example to one global maximum wastes compute on filler. Instead, a **data collator**, a function that stacks a list of examples into one batch, pads each batch only up to its own longest example as it is loaded. This is **dynamic padding**.

- `DataCollatorWithPadding(tok)` for classification and similar tasks.
- `DataCollatorForTokenClassification(tok)` also pads the per-token `labels` with `-100`.
- `DataCollatorForLanguageModeling(tok, mlm=False)` makes labels for training a causal language model (one that predicts the next token): the labels are simply the input tokens. With `mlm=True` it instead hides random tokens for a **masked language model** such as BERT, which learns to fill in blanks.
- `DataCollatorForSeq2Seq(tok, model=model)` for models that read one text and write another, such as translation models.

The label value **-100** is special: PyTorch's cross-entropy (and the loss functions in Transformers) skip it. So padding positions, and in chat training the instruction part of each example (the **prompt**, the text the model is answering), don't count toward the loss.

Name the target column `labels` (or `label`, which collators rename), because models compute the loss themselves when they receive `labels`. Remove the original text columns: the **Trainer**, Transformers' ready-made training loop (next lesson), drops unused columns anyway, but removing them yourself avoids surprises.

Putting examples of similar length in the same batch (`train_sampling_strategy="group_by_length"` in `TrainingArguments`) cuts padding further.
concepts.code:
from datasets import Dataset
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, DataCollatorWithPadding

tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("google-bert/bert-base-uncased")
ds = Dataset.from_dict({"text": ["short", "a much longer example sentence"],
                        "label": [0, 1]})

def tokenize(batch):
    return tok(batch["text"], truncation=True, max_length=128)

ds = ds.map(tokenize, batched=True, remove_columns=["text"])
print([len(x) for x in ds["input_ids"]])   # [3, 7]  (no padding yet)

collator = DataCollatorWithPadding(tok)
batch = collator([ds[0], ds[1]])
print(batch["input_ids"].shape)            # torch.Size([2, 7])  padded per batch
print(batch["labels"])                     # tensor([0, 1])  'label' renamed
takeaways: Tokenize with a batched `map` and truncation, but don't pad there
Data collators pad each batch only to its own longest example
Label -100 is skipped by the loss (padding, prompt tokens)
pitfalls: Padding everything to max_length in map, which makes training far slower than dynamic padding.

quiz.q: Why do token-classification collators pad labels with -100?
options: It is the ID of the pad token
The loss function ignores -100, so padded positions do not affect training
It marks the start of a sequence
quiz.explain: Cross-entropy uses ignore_index=-100, so padded or masked positions contribute nothing to the loss.

concepts.name: Fine-tuning with Trainer
concepts.summary: Configure TrainingArguments and run a complete fine-tuning loop with Trainer, including evaluation and checkpoints.
concepts.why: Trainer gives you a correct training loop, with mixed precision, multiple GPUs and progress reports built in, without writing it yourself.
concepts.body:
**Trainer** runs the whole PyTorch training loop for you: batching, forward and backward passes, the optimizer (AdamW by default), evaluation on a validation set, saving progress, printing progress reports, and using several GPUs.

It also lowers the learning rate step by step as training goes on. The object that does this is a **learning-rate scheduler**; by default it decreases the rate in a straight line down to zero, which usually trains better than a fixed rate.

You configure Trainer with `TrainingArguments`:

- `output_dir`: the folder for **checkpoints**, saved copies of the run's state made along the way.
- `learning_rate` (2e-5 to 5e-5 is typical for full fine-tuning), `num_train_epochs`, `per_device_train_batch_size` (the batch size on each GPU), `weight_decay`, and `warmup_steps`: a **warmup** that starts with a tiny learning rate and raises it over the first steps, to avoid wild early updates.
- `eval_strategy="epoch"` or `"steps"` and a matching `save_strategy`; `load_best_model_at_end=True` with `metric_for_best_model`.
- `logging_steps` sets how often it reports the loss; `report_to="none"`, or a tracking tool that draws charts of the run, such as `"tensorboard"`, `"wandb"` or `"mlflow"`.
- `bf16=True` on recent GPUs turns on **mixed precision**: most of the math runs in **bfloat16**, a 2-byte number format, which is faster and uses less memory.

Then:

```python
trainer = Trainer(model=model, args=args, train_dataset=train, eval_dataset=val,
                  processing_class=tok, data_collator=collator)
trainer.train()
```

`processing_class` (the tokenizer, or the matching preprocessor for images and audio) is saved with each checkpoint, so the checkpoint loads as a complete model. `trainer.evaluate()` returns a dict of metrics such as `eval_loss`; `trainer.predict(ds)` returns predictions, the true labels and metrics.

Resume an interrupted run with `trainer.train(resume_from_checkpoint=True)`. The model must return a loss when it is given `labels`, which every `AutoModelFor...` class does.
concepts.code:
from datasets import load_dataset
from transformers import (AutoModelForSequenceClassification, AutoTokenizer,
                          DataCollatorWithPadding, Trainer, TrainingArguments)

name = "distilbert/distilbert-base-uncased"
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(name)
model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(name, num_labels=2)

ds = load_dataset("stanfordnlp/imdb")
ds = ds.map(lambda b: tok(b["text"], truncation=True, max_length=256), batched=True)
train = ds["train"].shuffle(seed=42).select(range(2000))
val = ds["test"].shuffle(seed=42).select(range(500))

args = TrainingArguments(
    output_dir="imdb-distilbert", learning_rate=2e-5, num_train_epochs=2,
    per_device_train_batch_size=16, eval_strategy="epoch", save_strategy="epoch",
    load_best_model_at_end=True, logging_steps=50, report_to="none",
)
trainer = Trainer(model=model, args=args, train_dataset=train, eval_dataset=val,
                  processing_class=tok, data_collator=DataCollatorWithPadding(tok))
trainer.train()
print(trainer.evaluate())   # {'eval_loss': 0.3..., 'epoch': 2.0, ...}
takeaways: TrainingArguments configures; Trainer runs the loop
Pass `processing_class=tokenizer` so checkpoints include it
Match `eval_strategy` and `save_strategy` when using `load_best_model_at_end`
pitfalls: Using the removed argument name evaluation_strategy; current versions only accept eval_strategy.

quiz.q: You set load_best_model_at_end=True with eval_strategy='epoch' and save_strategy='steps'. What happens?
options: Trainer raises an error because the strategies must match
Only the last checkpoint is kept
Training works and keeps the best step
quiz.explain: The best model can only be restored if evaluation and saving happen on the same schedule.

concepts.name: Evaluation metrics
concepts.summary: Report accuracy, F1 and other metrics during training with a compute_metrics function.
concepts.why: The loss alone hides whether a model is useful; task metrics decide which checkpoint to keep and when to stop.
concepts.body:
By default `Trainer.evaluate()` reports only `eval_loss`. Pass a `compute_metrics` function to get task metrics. It receives an `EvalPrediction` with:

- `predictions`: the model's logits as NumPy arrays (for classification, shape `(n, num_labels)`),
- `label_ids`: the true labels.

It returns a dict of plain floats. The Trainer adds `eval_` to each key, so `{"f1": 0.9}` is reported as `eval_f1`; in `metric_for_best_model="f1"` (with `greater_is_better=True`) you still write the name without the prefix.

You can compute metrics with NumPy directly, with scikit-learn (a popular Python machine-learning toolkit), or with Hugging Face's `evaluate` library (`evaluate.load("accuracy")`).

Tips:

- For text generation or per-token tasks, the logits can be huge: one score per vocabulary entry for every token. `preprocess_logits_for_metrics` lets you shrink them (for example with `argmax`) on the GPU before they are collected, saving a lot of memory.
- For per-token labels, drop the positions whose label is -100 before scoring.
- Choose metrics that match the goal. When some classes are rare, plain accuracy looks good even if the model ignores them; use the **F1 score** averaged over classes (macro F1) instead.

The same function works with `trainer.predict(test_ds)`, which returns predictions, labels and metrics (with the prefix `test_`) for a final check on data the model never saw.
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, f1_score
from transformers import EvalPrediction

def compute_metrics(eval_pred: EvalPrediction):
    logits, labels = eval_pred.predictions, eval_pred.label_ids
    preds = np.argmax(logits, axis=-1)
    return {"accuracy": accuracy_score(labels, preds),
            "f1": f1_score(labels, preds, average="macro")}

# what Trainer would pass in after evaluation:
fake = EvalPrediction(predictions=np.array([[2.0, -1.0], [0.1, 0.3], [1.5, 0.2]]),
                      label_ids=np.array([0, 1, 1]))
print(compute_metrics(fake))   # {'accuracy': 0.666..., 'f1': 0.666...}

# Trainer(..., compute_metrics=compute_metrics) with
# TrainingArguments(metric_for_best_model="f1", greater_is_better=True, ...)
takeaways: `compute_metrics` gets logits and labels and returns a dict of floats
Logged keys get an `eval_` prefix; refer to them without it in `metric_for_best_model`
Use `preprocess_logits_for_metrics` to shrink large logits
pitfalls: Returning tensors or arrays instead of plain floats, which breaks the progress reports.

quiz.q: compute_metrics returns {'f1': 0.91}. Under which key does Trainer.evaluate() report it?
quiz.explain: Evaluation metrics get the eval_ prefix; predict() would use test_.

concepts.name: Saving, loading and pushing to the Hub
concepts.summary: Save fine-tuned models and tokenizers, reload them, and publish them to the Hub with a model card.
concepts.why: A model you cannot reload or share reproducibly is not finished.
concepts.body:
Every model, tokenizer and config has `save_pretrained(dir)` and `from_pretrained(dir)`. A saved folder contains `config.json`, `model.safetensors` (split into shards above a size limit), the tokenizer's files and the generation config. Always save the **tokenizer with the model**: a model folder without its tokenizer is a common bug once the model is put to use.

With `Trainer`:

- `trainer.save_model("final")` writes the model plus the `processing_class`.
- The checkpoints saved during training (`checkpoint-500/`) also hold the optimizer, the learning-rate scheduler and the random-number generator's state, so training can resume exactly; `save_total_limit=2` keeps only the latest two, to save disk space.

Sharing on the Hub:

- Log in with `hf auth login` (or set the `HF_TOKEN` environment variable).
- `model.push_to_hub("you/my-model")` and `tok.push_to_hub("you/my-model")` upload to a repo, creating it if needed; `private=True` keeps it private.
- `TrainingArguments(push_to_hub=True, hub_model_id=...)` uploads checkpoints during training, and `trainer.push_to_hub()` uploads the final model with an automatically written model card listing the settings and metrics.

Edit the model card (`README.md`) to describe the training data, what the model is meant for and its limits. Set `id2label` in the config before saving, so pipelines show readable labels.

To reload, point any `from_pretrained` or `pipeline(model=...)` at the local folder or the repo name.
concepts.code:
from transformers import AutoModelForSequenceClassification, AutoTokenizer, pipeline

name = "distilbert/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english"
model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(name)
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(name)

model.save_pretrained("my-sentiment")
tok.save_pretrained("my-sentiment")       # keep tokenizer next to weights
# my-sentiment/: config.json, model.safetensors, tokenizer.json, ...

clf = pipeline("text-classification", model="my-sentiment")
print(clf("Reloaded fine.")[0]["label"])  # POSITIVE

# after `hf auth login`:
# model.push_to_hub("your-name/my-sentiment", private=True)
# tok.push_to_hub("your-name/my-sentiment", private=True)
takeaways: `save_pretrained` saves and `from_pretrained` reloads models, tokenizers and configs
Training checkpoints add optimizer state for resuming; a final save needs only the model and tokenizer
`push_to_hub` publishes to a repo; describe the model in its model card
pitfalls: Saving only the model and later loading a different tokenizer, which silently gives the model the wrong token IDs.

quiz.q: What does a Trainer checkpoint-1000/ folder contain that a plain save_pretrained folder does not?
options: Optimizer, scheduler and random-number generator state for resuming training
quiz.explain: Checkpoints add the training state so train(resume_from_checkpoint=...) can continue exactly where it stopped.

concepts.name: Chat models and chat templates
concepts.summary: Format conversations with apply_chat_template so chat models see exactly the prompt format they were trained on.
concepts.why: Hand-built prompts for chat models hurt quality badly; templates make prompting correct and the same across models.
concepts.body:
An **instruct model** (or chat model) is an LLM fine-tuned further on example conversations, so it answers questions and follows instructions instead of just continuing text. In that training, every conversation was written out in one exact format, with special tokens marking who is speaking, such as `<|im_start|>user ... <|im_end|>`. Your prompts must use the same format, or quality drops badly.

You don't type that format yourself. Each chat model's tokenizer ships a **chat template**: a fill-in-the-blanks **template** (written in Jinja, a small template language) that turns a list of messages into exactly the text the model expects.

```python
messages = [{"role": "system", "content": "You are concise."},
            {"role": "user", "content": "What is a tensor?"}]
inputs = tok.apply_chat_template(messages, add_generation_prompt=True, return_tensors="pt")
```

- Each message has a `role`. The `system` message holds standing instructions about tone and rules, the **system prompt**; `user` is the person and `assistant` is the model.
- `add_generation_prompt=True` adds the marker that starts the assistant's turn, so the model replies instead of continuing the user's message.
- `tokenize=False` returns the formatted text so you can look at it.
- In version 5 the result is a dict (`input_ids`, `attention_mask`) by default, so pass it with `model.generate(**inputs)`.
- `tools=[...]` describes functions the model may ask your code to run, for models trained for **tool calling**. `continue_final_message=True` lets the model carry on an assistant reply you started yourself.

The `text-generation` pipeline applies the template automatically when you pass a list of messages, and returns the conversation with the new assistant message added.

Don't add the template's special tokens yourself and then tokenize with `add_special_tokens=True`: the start token would appear twice. When fine-tuning a chat model, format the training conversations with the same template.
concepts.code:
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, pipeline

repo = "HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-135M-Instruct"
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(repo)
messages = [{"role": "system", "content": "Answer in one sentence."},
            {"role": "user", "content": "What is gravity?"}]

print(tok.apply_chat_template(messages, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True))
# <|im_start|>system
# Answer in one sentence.<|im_end|>
# <|im_start|>user ... <|im_start|>assistant

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(repo)
inputs = tok.apply_chat_template(messages, add_generation_prompt=True, return_tensors="pt")
out = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=40)
print(tok.decode(out[0, inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]:], skip_special_tokens=True))

chat = pipeline("text-generation", model=repo)
reply = chat(messages, max_new_tokens=40)[0]["generated_text"][-1]
print(reply["role"])   # assistant
takeaways: Chat models need their own template; format messages with `apply_chat_template`
Use `add_generation_prompt=True` before generating a reply
Pipelines accept message lists and apply the template for you
pitfalls: Writing prompts as plain 'User: ... Assistant:' text for a chat model, which ignores the special tokens it was trained with.

quiz.q: What does add_generation_prompt=True do?
options: Appends the tokens that start an assistant turn so the model replies
quiz.explain: It ends the rendered prompt with the assistant header, signalling the model to answer as the assistant.

concepts.name: Decoding strategies and GenerationConfig
concepts.summary: Control output quality and variety with greedy decoding, sampling, temperature, top-p, beam search and stopping rules.
concepts.why: The same model writes repetitive, creative or nonsensical text depending on its decoding settings.
concepts.body:
At each step the model gives every token in its vocabulary a probability of coming next. The **decoding strategy** decides which token to actually take.

- **Greedy** (`do_sample=False`, `num_beams=1`): always the most likely token. The same prompt always gives the same output, which suits short factual answers, but long texts tend to repeat themselves.
- **Sampling** (`do_sample=True`): a random draw, weighted by the probabilities. A **temperature** below 1 makes likely tokens even likelier (safer text); above 1 it evens the odds out (more surprising text). **top-p** (`top_p=0.9`, also called nucleus sampling) draws only from the most likely tokens that together cover 90% of the probability; **top-k** (`top_k=50`) draws from the 50 most likely; `min_p` drops tokens far less likely than the top one.
- **Beam search** (`num_beams=4`): follows several candidate continuations at once and keeps the best overall. Useful for outputs with one right answer, such as translation; rarely for open chat.

Other useful settings: `repetition_penalty` (e.g. 1.1) makes already-used tokens less likely, `no_repeat_ngram_size=3` forbids repeating any run of 3 tokens, `stop_strings=["\n\n"]` stops at given text (pass `tokenizer=tok` to `generate` too), plus `eos_token_id` and `num_return_sequences`.

These settings live in a `GenerationConfig`. The checkpoint's `generation_config.json` gives the defaults (many models tuned for chat default to sampling at a set temperature), arguments to `generate` override them, and `model.generation_config.save_pretrained(dir)` saves your own.

Call `transformers.set_seed(0)` to make sampling repeatable. When comparing models, use greedy decoding or a fixed seed, so differences come from the models and not from luck.
concepts.code:
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, GenerationConfig, set_seed

repo = "HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-135M"
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(repo)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(repo)
inputs = tok("Once upon a time", return_tensors="pt")

greedy = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=30, do_sample=False)

set_seed(0)
creative = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=30, do_sample=True,
                          temperature=0.8, top_p=0.9, repetition_penalty=1.1)

stop = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=60, stop_strings=["."], tokenizer=tok)
print(tok.decode(stop[0], skip_special_tokens=True))   # ends at the first period

cfg = GenerationConfig(max_new_tokens=50, do_sample=True, temperature=0.7, top_p=0.95)
out = model.generate(**inputs, generation_config=cfg)
print(model.generation_config.eos_token_id)   # checkpoint default, e.g. 0
takeaways: Greedy always gives the same output; sampling with temperature/top-p adds variety
The checkpoint's generation_config.json sets defaults that generate() arguments override
Use `stop_strings` (with `tokenizer=`) and repetition settings to shape outputs
pitfalls: Setting temperature without do_sample=True: it has no effect under greedy decoding, and the library prints a warning.

quiz.q: You set temperature=0.3 but leave do_sample=False. What happens?
options: Temperature is ignored because greedy decoding does not sample
quiz.explain: Temperature only reshapes the sampling distribution; with sampling off, the argmax token is always taken.

concepts.name: LoRA fine-tuning with PEFT
concepts.summary: Fine-tune large models cheaply by training small low-rank adapters with the PEFT library.
concepts.why: LoRA cuts the number of trained parameters by 100x or more, so fine-tuning an LLM fits on a single GPU.
concepts.body:
Full fine-tuning updates every weight, and needs memory for a gradient and the optimizer's extra numbers for each one. For a model with billions of weights, that means many GPUs.

**LoRA** (Low-Rank Adaptation) avoids this. It **freezes** the original weights, meaning they get no gradients and never change, and learns a small correction for some of the linear layers. Each correction is the product of two thin matrices, `B @ A`, whose result has the same shape as the layer's weight matrix `W`; the layer then computes with `W + (alpha / r) * B @ A`. The inner size `r` is small (8 to 64), so `A` and `B` together are usually well under 1% of the model's parameters, and only they are trained. These small trained add-ons are called **adapters**.

With Hugging Face's **PEFT** library (parameter-efficient fine-tuning, `pip install peft`):

```python
config = LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, lora_dropout=0.05,
                    target_modules=["q_proj", "v_proj"], task_type="CAUSAL_LM")
model = get_peft_model(model, config)
model.print_trainable_parameters()
```

- `target_modules` names the layers to adapt. Names differ between model families: Llama-style models call two parts of their attention layers `q_proj` and `v_proj`, BERT calls them `query` and `value`. `"all-linear"` adapts every linear layer and often works best.
- Use a higher learning rate than for full fine-tuning (around 1e-4 to 2e-4).
- The wrapped model works with `Trainer` unchanged.

`model.save_pretrained(dir)` saves only the adapter, a few megabytes. Load it later with `PeftModel.from_pretrained(base_model, dir)`, or call `merge_and_unload()` to add the adapter into the original weights for good, so you can ship the model without needing PEFT. You can also load several adapters onto one original model and switch between them, for example one per customer.
concepts.code:
from peft import LoraConfig, PeftModel, get_peft_model
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM

base = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-135M")
config = LoraConfig(
    r=16, lora_alpha=32, lora_dropout=0.05,
    target_modules=["q_proj", "v_proj"], task_type="CAUSAL_LM",
)
model = get_peft_model(base, config)
model.print_trainable_parameters()
# trainable params: ... || all params: ... || trainable%: well under 1%

# ... train with Trainer(model=model, ...) as usual, lr around 2e-4 ...

model.save_pretrained("smol-lora")            # adapter only: a few MB

base = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-135M")
tuned = PeftModel.from_pretrained(base, "smol-lora")
merged = tuned.merge_and_unload()             # plain model, adapter folded in
merged.save_pretrained("smol-merged")
takeaways: LoRA freezes the original weights and trains small add-on matrices
`target_modules` must match the model's layer names (or use `all-linear`)
Adapters are a few MB; `merge_and_unload` folds them into the weights for shipping
pitfalls: Copying target_modules=['q_proj', 'v_proj'] to a BERT model, where those layer names do not exist, which raises an error.

quiz.q: After get_peft_model with LoRA, which weights receive gradient updates?
options: Only the low-rank adapter matrices (plus any modules you mark trainable)
quiz.explain: The base model is frozen; only adapter parameters (and explicitly listed modules) are trained.

concepts.name: Quantized loading
concepts.summary: Load models in 8-bit or 4-bit with bitsandbytes, and know when other methods such as GPTQ, AWQ or torchao fit better.
concepts.why: Quantization lets a 7-billion-parameter model run in about 5 GB of GPU memory instead of 14 GB.
concepts.body:
Each weight normally takes 2 bytes in **bfloat16** (bf16), the usual 16-bit format, so a model with 7 billion weights needs about 14 GB (**gigabytes**, billions of bytes) just to hold them. **Quantization** stores weights in fewer bits: 8 bits halves that, 4 bits quarters it, at a modest cost in accuracy.

Transformers loads quantized models through a `quantization_config`:

```python
bnb = BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_4bit=True, bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4",
                         bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
                         bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(repo, quantization_config=bnb, device_map="auto")
```

**bitsandbytes** quantizes the weights while they load, needs no sample data to tune with, and is the basis of QLoRA, fine-tuning on top of a 4-bit model (next lesson). **NF4** is a 4-bit format designed for neural-network weights, which mostly sit near zero in a bell-curve shape. The compute dtype is the format the matrix multiplications run in after the 4-bit weights are expanded back.

Other families:

- **Pre-quantized checkpoints**, made ahead of time with methods such as **GPTQ** or **AWQ**, or stored in `compressed-tensors`, FP8 or MXFP4 formats, load directly from repos that ship them; the settings are read from the checkpoint. They are often faster for inference than bitsandbytes.
- **torchao**, PyTorch's own quantization library, offers 8-bit and 4-bit integer and 8-bit float formats and works with `torch.compile`.

Trade-offs: fewer bits mean less memory but some loss of quality. Speed depends on whether fast GPU code exists for that format on your hardware, and quantized inference is not always faster than bf16. Test on your own task. Note that the old `load_in_8bit=True` argument to `from_pretrained` is gone; always pass a config object.
concepts.code:
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, BitsAndBytesConfig

repo = "Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct"

bnb4 = BitsAndBytesConfig(
    load_in_4bit=True,
    bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4",
    bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
    bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True,
)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    repo, quantization_config=bnb4, device_map="auto")   # needs a CUDA GPU

print(f"{model.get_memory_footprint() / 1e9:.1f} GB")    # roughly 5 GB vs ~15 GB in bf16

bnb8 = BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_8bit=True)
# model8 = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(repo, quantization_config=bnb8, device_map="auto")

# pre-quantized checkpoints carry their own config:
# AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-AWQ", device_map="auto")
takeaways: Pass a `quantization_config` (e.g. `BitsAndBytesConfig`) to `from_pretrained`
4-bit NF4 with bf16 compute is the usual QLoRA setup
Pre-quantized GPTQ/AWQ/FP8 checkpoints load directly and are often faster
pitfalls: Expecting quantization to always speed up inference; it mainly saves memory, and speed depends on the GPU code available.

quiz.q: Roughly how much GPU memory do the weights of an 8B-parameter model take in 4-bit?
quiz.explain: 4 bits is half a byte per parameter: about 4 GB, plus some overhead for scales and unquantized layers.

concepts.name: QLoRA: LoRA on a 4-bit base
concepts.summary: Combine 4-bit quantized original weights with LoRA adapters to fine-tune large models on a single GPU.
concepts.why: QLoRA is the standard recipe for fine-tuning 7B to 70B models on modest hardware.
concepts.body:
**QLoRA** loads the original model in 4-bit NF4 with bitsandbytes and trains LoRA adapters in higher precision on top. The frozen weights take a quarter of their bf16 memory, and gradients flow only into the small adapters, so a 7-billion-parameter model fine-tunes comfortably on a 24 GB GPU.

The recipe:

1. Load the model with a 4-bit `BitsAndBytesConfig` (`nf4`, bf16 compute, double quantization).
2. Call `prepare_model_for_kbit_training(model)` from PEFT. It turns on **gradient checkpointing**, which saves memory by recomputing each layer's intermediate results during the backward pass instead of storing them. It also makes the inputs require gradients, which checkpointing needs when the weights are frozen, and converts the layer norms to float32 for stability.
3. Apply a `LoraConfig` with `target_modules="all-linear"`; adapting every linear layer recovers most of the quality of full fine-tuning.
4. Train with `Trainer` using `bf16=True`, an optimizer such as `optim="paged_adamw_8bit"` (AdamW that keeps its extra numbers in 8 bits), and a learning rate around 2e-4.

To ship the result, you can't add an adapter straight into 4-bit weights without losing precision. The usual way: reload the original model in bf16, load the adapter, call `merge_and_unload()`, and then, if you like, quantize the merged model again with a method suited to inference.

For teaching a model to follow instructions from example answers, Hugging Face's **TRL** library has `SFTTrainer` (supervised fine-tuning), which wraps this recipe: it accepts a `peft_config`, formats conversations with the model's chat template (its built-in conversation format), and packs several short examples into one sequence to avoid padding.
concepts.code:
import torch
from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model, prepare_model_for_kbit_training
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, BitsAndBytesConfig, TrainingArguments

bnb = BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_4bit=True, bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4",
                         bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
                         bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    "Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B", quantization_config=bnb, device_map="auto")

model = prepare_model_for_kbit_training(model)   # grad checkpointing, fp32 norms
model = get_peft_model(model, LoraConfig(
    r=16, lora_alpha=32, lora_dropout=0.05,
    target_modules="all-linear", task_type="CAUSAL_LM"))

args = TrainingArguments(
    output_dir="qwen-qlora", per_device_train_batch_size=4,
    gradient_accumulation_steps=4, learning_rate=2e-4, num_train_epochs=1,
    bf16=True, optim="paged_adamw_8bit", logging_steps=10, report_to="none",
)
# Trainer(model=model, args=args, train_dataset=..., data_collator=...).train()
takeaways: QLoRA = frozen 4-bit NF4 weights + LoRA adapters trained in bf16
Call `prepare_model_for_kbit_training` before adding adapters
Merge adapters into a bf16 reload of the model, not into 4-bit weights
pitfalls: Merging an adapter directly into the 4-bit weights and shipping that, which loses precision compared with merging into bf16 weights.

quiz.q: Why does QLoRA use NF4 for the original weights but bf16 for the adapters?
options: bf16 uses less memory than NF4
The frozen weights only need compact storage, while the trained adapters need precise gradients
Adapters cannot be quantized at all
quiz.explain: The original weights are never updated, so heavy compression is fine; the small trained parameters stay in higher precision.

concepts.name: Memory and speed in training
concepts.summary: Fit bigger models and batches with mixed precision, gradient accumulation, gradient checkpointing and better optimizers.
concepts.why: Running out of GPU memory and slow epochs are the main practical obstacles in fine-tuning.
concepts.body:
Training memory has four parts: the weights, their gradients, the optimizer state (AdamW keeps two extra numbers per weight) and the **activations**, the intermediate results each layer produces, which are kept for the backward pass. When they don't fit, training stops with an **out-of-memory** (OOM) error. `TrainingArguments` exposes the standard levers:

- **Mixed precision**: `bf16=True` (NVIDIA GPUs from the 2020 Ampere generation on) runs most math in bfloat16, faster and lighter. `fp16=True` is for older GPUs; it automatically scales the loss up so tiny gradients don't round to zero.
- **Gradient accumulation**: `gradient_accumulation_steps=8` with `per_device_train_batch_size=2` adds up the gradients of 8 small batches before each optimizer step, the effect of a batch of 16 per device with the activation memory of 2.
- **Gradient checkpointing**: `gradient_checkpointing=True` throws activations away and recomputes them in the backward pass, cutting activation memory a lot for roughly 20 to 30% more compute.
- **Optimizers**: `optim="adamw_torch_fused"` is faster; `"adamw_bnb_8bit"` or `"paged_adamw_8bit"` keep the optimizer state in 8 bits; `"adafactor"` uses even less.
- **Throughput** (examples per second): `train_sampling_strategy="group_by_length"`, `dataloader_num_workers` (prepare the next batches while the GPU works), `torch_compile=True` (compile the model for speed), and, for LLM training, packing several short examples into one sequence so no compute goes to pad tokens.

A practical OOM checklist: turn on bf16, halve the batch and double the accumulation, turn on gradient checkpointing, shorten `max_length`, switch to an 8-bit optimizer, then move to LoRA or QLoRA, which train small add-on weights instead of the whole model.

`auto_find_batch_size=True` makes Trainer try again with a smaller batch after an OOM error. Remember that the effective batch size changes the best learning rate.
concepts.code:
from transformers import TrainingArguments

args = TrainingArguments(
    output_dir="out",
    per_device_train_batch_size=4,
    gradient_accumulation_steps=8,      # effective batch 32 per device
    bf16=True,                          # mixed precision (Ampere+ GPUs)
    gradient_checkpointing=True,        # trade compute for activation memory
    optim="adamw_torch_fused",
    learning_rate=2e-5,
    warmup_steps=100,
    lr_scheduler_type="cosine",
    train_sampling_strategy="group_by_length",  # less padding per batch
    dataloader_num_workers=4,
    report_to="none",
)
eff = args.per_device_train_batch_size * args.gradient_accumulation_steps
print(eff)   # 32
takeaways: Weights, gradients, optimizer state and activations all consume memory
Gradient accumulation raises effective batch size without more activation memory
Gradient checkpointing and 8-bit optimizers are the next levers after bf16
pitfalls: Raising gradient_accumulation_steps without adjusting the learning rate, then wondering why training dynamics changed.

quiz.q: per_device_train_batch_size=2, gradient_accumulation_steps=16, 4 GPUs. What is the effective global batch size?
quiz.explain: 2 per device x 16 accumulation steps x 4 devices = 128 examples per optimizer step.

concepts.name: Callbacks and custom training logic
concepts.summary: Extend Trainer with callbacks, early stopping, a custom loss and your own optimizer without rewriting the loop.
concepts.why: Real projects need class weights, special losses or extra reporting; Trainer has a place to plug in each one.
concepts.body:
`Trainer` is designed to be extended rather than replaced.

**Callbacks** watch training and can steer it. Subclass `TrainerCallback` and implement event methods such as `on_log`, `on_evaluate`, `on_epoch_end` or `on_step_end`, which Trainer calls at those moments. They receive `args`, `state` (step, epoch, the reported values so far, the best metric) and `control`, whose flags such as `control.should_stop = True` change what happens next. Built-ins include `EarlyStoppingCallback(early_stopping_patience=3)`, which stops when the metric hasn't improved for 3 evaluations; it needs `load_best_model_at_end=True` and a `metric_for_best_model`. Callbacks for tracking tools such as TensorBoard, Weights & Biases or MLflow are added through `report_to`.

**Custom loss**: subclass `Trainer` and override `compute_loss(self, model, inputs, return_outputs=False, num_items_in_batch=None)`, for example to apply class weights that make mistakes on a rare class cost more. Pop the labels, run the model, compute the loss, and return `(loss, outputs)` when `return_outputs` is true. Or pass `compute_loss_func=` when you create the Trainer.

**Custom optimizer and scheduler**: pass `optimizers=(optimizer, scheduler)`, or override `create_optimizer`, for example to give the backbone and the head different learning rates.

Callbacks shouldn't change the model or the data; keep them for reporting and control. For a fundamentally different loop, such as reinforcement learning (learning from rewards rather than labelled answers), look at Hugging Face's TRL library, or write a plain PyTorch loop with Accelerate, the library that handles devices and multiple GPUs for hand-written loops.
concepts.code:
import torch
from transformers import EarlyStoppingCallback, Trainer, TrainerCallback

class WeightedLossTrainer(Trainer):
    def compute_loss(self, model, inputs, return_outputs=False, num_items_in_batch=None):
        labels = inputs.pop("labels")
        outputs = model(**inputs)
        weights = torch.tensor([1.0, 4.0], device=outputs.logits.device)  # rare class x4
        loss = torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy(outputs.logits, labels, weight=weights)
        return (loss, outputs) if return_outputs else loss

class PrintEval(TrainerCallback):
    def on_evaluate(self, args, state, control, metrics=None, **kwargs):
        print(f"epoch {state.epoch}: {metrics.get('eval_f1')}")

# trainer = WeightedLossTrainer(
#     model=model, args=args,  # args: load_best_model_at_end=True, metric_for_best_model="f1"
#     train_dataset=train, eval_dataset=val, compute_metrics=compute_metrics,
#     callbacks=[EarlyStoppingCallback(early_stopping_patience=2), PrintEval()],
# )
takeaways: Callbacks watch training events and can stop it or change what happens next via `control`
Override `compute_loss` (or pass `compute_loss_func`) for custom losses
EarlyStoppingCallback needs `load_best_model_at_end` and `metric_for_best_model`
