pitfalls: Forgetting to return (loss, outputs) when return_outputs=True, which breaks evaluation and prediction.

quiz.q: What must be configured for EarlyStoppingCallback to work?
options: load_best_model_at_end=True and a metric_for_best_model, with periodic evaluation
quiz.explain: Early stopping tracks an evaluation metric across evaluations and needs the best-model machinery enabled.

concepts.name: KV cache and streaming output
concepts.summary: Understand the key-value cache that makes generation fast, choose a cache type, and stream text as it is produced.
concepts.why: Generation speed and memory are dominated by the KV cache, and streaming is what makes chat apps feel responsive.
concepts.body:
Inside each attention layer, every token is turned into a **key** (what it offers for others to match against) and a **value** (the information it passes on). Each new token compares itself with the keys of all earlier tokens. Recomputing those keys and values at every step would make each step slower as the text grows, so models store them in a **KV cache**. The first forward pass, the **prefill**, runs the whole prompt and fills the cache; each later decode step runs just the one new token and appends its keys and values.

The cache grows with layers x attention heads (separate attention calculations side by side within a layer) x text length x batch size. For long texts it can take more memory than the weights. Transformers offers several cache classes:

- `DynamicCache` (default): grows as needed.
- `StaticCache` (`cache_implementation="static"`): reserves a fixed maximum length up front, so tensor shapes never change. That lets `torch.compile`, which turns a model into faster code, build a much faster decode step.
- Offloaded caches move part of the cache to CPU memory, and others store it with fewer bits per number; both save GPU memory at some cost in speed. Sliding-window models keep only the most recent tokens.

You can reuse a cache across calls: pass `past_key_values=` to continue from a shared beginning, such as a long system prompt, instead of processing it again.

**Streaming** shows the text piece by piece as it is generated, like a chatbot typing its answer. `TextStreamer(tok)` prints to the terminal. `TextIteratorStreamer` hands the pieces to your code instead, but `generate` doesn't return until it has finished, so run it in a separate **thread** (a second line of execution inside your program) and read the streamer in the original one, for example to push each piece to a web page.

To serve many users at once, dedicated serving engines (vLLM, TGI, SGLang) or `transformers serve` beat calling `generate` per message: they keep merging new users' messages into the running batch (continuous batching) and store the cache in small blocks (paged attention).
concepts.code:
from threading import Thread
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, TextIteratorStreamer

repo = "HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-135M-Instruct"
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(repo)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(repo)
msgs = [{"role": "user", "content": "Name three planets."}]
inputs = tok.apply_chat_template(msgs, add_generation_prompt=True, return_tensors="pt")

streamer = TextIteratorStreamer(tok, skip_prompt=True, skip_special_tokens=True)
thread = Thread(target=model.generate,
                kwargs=dict(**inputs, max_new_tokens=40, streamer=streamer))
thread.start()
for chunk in streamer:          # text arrives as it is generated
    print(chunk, end="", flush=True)
thread.join()

# static cache: fixed shapes, compile-friendly decode step
out = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=40, cache_implementation="static")
takeaways: Prefill fills the KV cache; each decode step adds one token's keys and values
StaticCache gives fixed shapes for torch.compile; DynamicCache is the flexible default
Stream with TextIteratorStreamer and run generate in a separate thread
pitfalls: Iterating a TextIteratorStreamer in the same thread that calls generate, which blocks until generation is over.

quiz.q: Why does generation slow down and use more memory for very long conversations?
options: The KV cache grows with sequence length and every new token attends over it
quiz.explain: Cache memory and attention cost per step both scale with the number of cached tokens.

concepts.name: Attention backends and device placement
concepts.summary: Choose sdpa, FlashAttention or custom attention code, and control how a model is spread over GPUs, CPU and disk.
concepts.why: The attention code and the model's placement decide whether a long-text model is fast, slow or fits at all.
concepts.body:
Attention is the most expensive operation in a transformer, because every token is compared with every other one. Transformers keeps the model code separate from the code that actually computes attention, the **attention implementation**, chosen with `attn_implementation` when loading:

- `"sdpa"` (default when supported): PyTorch's built-in `scaled_dot_product_attention`, which automatically picks a fast, memory-saving GPU routine when one fits, often a FlashAttention-style one.
- `"flash_attention_2"` / `"flash_attention_3"`: the separate FlashAttention packages, which compute attention in small tiles and never store the full table of scores. Very fast on supported NVIDIA GPUs; they need weights in one of the two 16-bit number formats (float16 or bfloat16) and allow **padding-free** training, where examples are packed back to back with no pad tokens.
- `"flex_attention"`: PyTorch's attention that you can customise, for example with unusual masks.
- `"eager"`: plain step-by-step PyTorch code. Slow, but the only one that can return the attention scores (`output_attentions=True`), and the easiest to step through when hunting a bug.

Through the **attention interface** you can register your own function (`AttentionInterface.register`) or load ready-made attention code from the Hub, and switch a loaded model with `model.set_attn_implementation(...)`.

**Placement**: `device_map="auto"` uses Accelerate to fill the GPUs in order, then CPU RAM, then disk; `max_memory={0: "20GiB", "cpu": "60GiB"}` sets the budgets. Layers moved off the GPU work but are slow, because their weights are copied over the link between CPU and GPU on every forward pass. `model.hf_device_map` shows where each layer went.

`device_map="auto"` splits the layers across GPUs in sequence, like stations on an assembly line, so only one GPU is busy at a time. To make all GPUs work on every layer at once (**tensor parallelism**, splitting each layer's matrices across them), load with `tp_plan="auto"` and launch with `torchrun`.

Time your own workload before switching: gains depend on text length, batch size, dtype and GPU generation.
concepts.code:
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM

repo = "Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct"

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    repo, dtype=torch.bfloat16, attn_implementation="sdpa", device_map="auto",
    max_memory={0: "6GiB", "cpu": "24GiB"},   # spill to CPU beyond 6 GiB of GPU 0
)
print(model.config._attn_implementation)   # sdpa
print(set(model.hf_device_map.values()))   # e.g. {0} or {0, 'cpu'}

# eager attention is required to inspect attention weights
eager = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(repo, attn_implementation="eager")
ids = torch.tensor([[1, 2, 3]])
att = eager(ids, output_attentions=True).attentions
print(len(att), att[0].shape)   # num_layers, (batch, heads, seq, seq)

# FlashAttention (needs the flash-attn package, fp16/bf16, supported GPU):
# AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(repo, dtype=torch.bfloat16,
#                                      attn_implementation="flash_attention_2")
takeaways: `attn_implementation` selects sdpa, flash_attention_2/3, flex_attention or `eager`
Only `eager` returns attention scores; the fast versions never store them
`device_map="auto"` with `max_memory` places layers across GPUs, CPU and disk
pitfalls: Assuming device_map='auto' across two GPUs doubles speed; it splits layers sequentially, so only one GPU works at a time.

quiz.q: You need output_attentions=True for a study of what the model attends to. Which implementation should you load?
quiz.explain: The fast implementations never store the full table of attention scores, so only eager can return it.

concepts.name: Multi-GPU training: DDP, FSDP, DeepSpeed
concepts.summary: Scale Trainer runs across GPUs and machines with torchrun or accelerate, using DDP, FSDP or DeepSpeed ZeRO.
concepts.why: Models that don't fit on one GPU, or runs that would take days on one, need training spread across many GPUs.
concepts.body:
`Trainer` can train on many GPUs with no code changes; what changes is **how you start** the script. Each GPU is driven by its own copy of your program, a separate **process**, and the processes talk to each other to stay in step. Each process has a number, its **rank** (0, 1, 2 ...), and the number of processes is the **world size**.

- **DDP** (DistributedDataParallel): `torchrun --nproc_per_node=4 train.py`, where **torchrun** is PyTorch's launcher that starts one process per GPU. Each GPU holds a full copy of the model and works on a different slice of each batch; after the backward pass the GPUs average their gradients, so all copies stay identical. Simple and fast, but the model plus its optimizer state must fit on one GPU.
- **FSDP** (Fully Sharded Data Parallel): splits the parameters, gradients and optimizer state into shards, one per GPU, and gathers each layer's full weights only for the moment it is needed. Turn it on with `TrainingArguments(fsdp="full_shard auto_wrap", fsdp_config={...})` or an `accelerate config` file. Memory per GPU drops roughly by the number of GPUs.
- **DeepSpeed ZeRO**: `TrainingArguments(deepspeed="ds_config.json")`. Stage 1 splits the optimizer state, stage 2 also the gradients, stage 3 also the parameters; it can also move parts to CPU memory or fast local disks.

What changes in a multi-GPU run:

- `per_device_train_batch_size` is per GPU; the **global batch** behind each optimizer step is that times the world size (times any gradient accumulation).
- Only rank 0 should write files or print. Trainer handles this; in your own code check `trainer.is_world_process_zero()`.
- Saving a sharded model means first collecting the full weights onto rank 0 (FSDP's state-dict settings do this).
- Each process must see different data; Trainer splits the dataset for you.

`accelerate launch` reads a saved setup and works on one machine or several. Start with DDP; move to FSDP or ZeRO-3 only when memory forces you to.
concepts.code:
# train.py stays the same Trainer script; only the launch and the arguments change.
from transformers import TrainingArguments

fsdp_args = TrainingArguments(
    output_dir="out-fsdp",
    per_device_train_batch_size=2,       # global batch = 2 x world size x accumulation
    gradient_accumulation_steps=4,
    bf16=True,
    fsdp="full_shard auto_wrap",
    fsdp_config={"transformer_layer_cls_to_wrap": ["Qwen2DecoderLayer"]},
    report_to="none",
)
# DeepSpeed alternative: TrainingArguments(..., deepspeed="ds_zero3.json")

# Launch commands (shell):
#   torchrun --nproc_per_node=4 train.py              # DDP or FSDP on 4 GPUs
#   accelerate config && accelerate launch train.py   # saved launch setup
#   torchrun --nnodes=2 --nproc_per_node=8 --rdzv_backend=c10d \
#            --rdzv_endpoint=host0:29500 train.py     # 2 machines x 8 GPUs
takeaways: Trainer code is unchanged; launch with torchrun or accelerate
DDP keeps a full model copy per GPU; FSDP and ZeRO-3 split parameters, gradients and optimizer state
Batch size arguments are per GPU; the global batch grows with the world size
pitfalls: Writing files or printing from every rank, which produces garbled or duplicated output.

quiz.q: A model plus its Adam state needs 60 GB; you have 4 GPUs with 24 GB each. Which approach can train it?
options: FSDP full sharding or DeepSpeed ZeRO-3
quiz.explain: DDP needs everything on each GPU; splitting parameters, gradients and optimizer state spreads 60 GB over 96 GB.

concepts.name: Tokenizer internals and training
concepts.summary: Learn a tokenizer's four stages, how BPE, WordPiece and Unigram differ, and how to train a new tokenizer.
concepts.why: Specialised text, mapping predictions back to characters and multilingual quirks all require looking inside the tokenizer.
concepts.body:
A fast (Rust-based) tokenizer runs four stages:

1. **Normalization**: cleaning the text first, such as making equivalent characters identical in Unicode, the standard that numbers every character ("é" can be stored as one character or as "e" plus an accent mark), lowercasing or removing accents. BERT-uncased lowercases; most LLMs do not.
2. **Pre-tokenization**: splitting into words, or into byte-sized chunks. GPT-style byte-level BPE gives every possible byte its own symbol, so no input is ever unknown.
3. **Model**: the subword method. **BPE** (byte-pair encoding) repeatedly merges the most frequent pair of neighbouring symbols (GPT, Llama, Qwen); **WordPiece** is similar but picks merges by how much they help, and marks continuations with `##` (BERT); **Unigram** starts from a very large vocabulary and removes the least useful pieces (T5, through the SentencePiece library).
4. **Post-processing**: adds special tokens such as `[CLS]`/`[SEP]` or a start token.

`tok.backend_tokenizer` exposes these components. `return_offsets_mapping=True` returns each token's start and end character, essential for mapping predictions back to the text in named-entity recognition (NER) or in question answering that points at the answer inside a passage; `enc.word_ids()` maps tokens to words.

For a new kind of text (code, chemistry, a new language), `tok.train_new_from_iterator(texts, vocab_size=...)` trains a tokenizer **with the same stages and special tokens** on your texts. A new tokenizer means new token IDs, so the model's embeddings no longer match them; that only makes sense when training a model from scratch. To keep a pretrained model, add a few tokens instead with `tok.add_tokens([...])` and `model.resize_token_embeddings(len(tok))`.

Watch the spaces: byte-level BPE folds a leading space into the token, so `"hello"` and `" hello"` get different IDs.
concepts.code:
from tokenizers import Tokenizer, models, normalizers, pre_tokenizers, trainers
from transformers import PreTrainedTokenizerFast

corpus = ["the cat sat on the mat", "the cats sat", "a matter of cats"] * 50

raw = Tokenizer(models.WordPiece(unk_token="[UNK]"))
raw.normalizer = normalizers.Lowercase()
raw.pre_tokenizer = pre_tokenizers.Whitespace()
raw.train_from_iterator(corpus, trainers.WordPieceTrainer(
    vocab_size=60, special_tokens=["[UNK]", "[PAD]"]))

tok = PreTrainedTokenizerFast(tokenizer_object=raw, unk_token="[UNK]", pad_token="[PAD]")
enc = tok("The Cats sat", return_offsets_mapping=True)
print(tok.convert_ids_to_tokens(enc["input_ids"]))  # ['the', 'cats', 'sat']
print(enc["offset_mapping"])          # [(0, 3), (4, 8), (9, 12)]
print(enc.word_ids())                 # [0, 1, 2]
print(tok.tokenize("matters"))        # ['matter', '##s']
# pretrained = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("gpt2")
# new_tok = pretrained.train_new_from_iterator(my_texts, vocab_size=32000)
takeaways: Pipeline: normalize, pre-tokenize, subword model (BPE/WordPiece/Unigram), post-process
Offsets and word_ids map tokens back to character spans and words
A newly trained tokenizer needs a newly trained model; add tokens to extend an existing one
pitfalls: Training a new tokenizer for an existing pretrained model, which scrambles the mapping between token IDs and learned embeddings.

quiz.q: You add 50 domain terms with tok.add_tokens(...). What else must you do before fine-tuning?
quiz.explain: New token IDs need rows in the embedding matrix; resizing adds them (initialised, then learned during fine-tuning).

concepts.name: Model classes, configs and custom models
concepts.summary: See how PreTrainedConfig, PreTrainedModel and task heads fit together, and register your own architecture with the Auto classes.
concepts.why: Tracking down odd model behaviour, adding a custom head, or shipping a new model design requires knowing these building blocks.
concepts.body:
Every model design in Transformers is built from three pieces:

- A **config** class (subclass of `PreTrainedConfig`) holding settings such as hidden size, number of layers, attention heads and vocabulary size; it is what gets saved as `config.json`.
- A **base model** (`LlamaModel`, `BertModel`) subclassing `PreTrainedModel`, which adds `from_pretrained`, `save_pretrained`, weight initialisation, embedding resizing, gradient checkpointing (recomputing activations to save memory) and Hub support on top of `torch.nn.Module`.
- **Heads** (`LlamaForCausalLM`, `BertForSequenceClassification`) that wrap the base model and return `ModelOutput` dataclasses, including a `loss` when labels are given.

The library deliberately repeats code in each model ("single model, single file") so every modeling file can be read on its own. In the library's source code, **modular** files let a new model inherit from existing ones; a script expands them into standalone files.

To build your own:

1. Subclass `PreTrainedConfig` with a unique `model_type`.
2. Subclass `PreTrainedModel`, set `config_class`, and implement `forward`.
3. Register them: `AutoConfig.register("my-model", MyConfig)` and `AutoModel.register(MyConfig, MyModel)`.

Now `save_pretrained` and `from_pretrained` work, and with `register_for_auto_class()` plus `push_to_hub` others can load it with `trust_remote_code=True`.

Reading a model's modeling file is the fastest way to answer questions like "where is RoPE, the position encoding, stretched for longer texts?" or "which layer names should LoRA target?"
concepts.code:
import torch
from torch import nn
from transformers import AutoConfig, AutoModel, PreTrainedConfig, PreTrainedModel

class TinyConfig(PreTrainedConfig):
    model_type = "tiny-mlp"
    def __init__(self, in_dim=4, hidden=8, num_labels=2, **kwargs):
        self.in_dim, self.hidden = in_dim, hidden
        super().__init__(num_labels=num_labels, **kwargs)

class TinyModel(PreTrainedModel):
    config_class = TinyConfig
    def __init__(self, config):
        super().__init__(config)
        self.net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(config.in_dim, config.hidden), nn.ReLU(),
                                 nn.Linear(config.hidden, config.num_labels))
        self.post_init()
    def forward(self, x):
        return {"logits": self.net(x)}

AutoConfig.register("tiny-mlp", TinyConfig)
AutoModel.register(TinyConfig, TinyModel)
TinyModel(TinyConfig()).save_pretrained("tiny")
model = AutoModel.from_pretrained("tiny")
print(type(model).__name__, model(torch.ones(1, 4))["logits"].shape)  # TinyModel torch.Size([1, 2])
takeaways: Config + PreTrainedModel base + task heads make up every architecture
Register custom configs and models with the Auto classes to get save/load for free
Modeling files are intentionally self-contained; read them to track down odd behaviour
pitfalls: Forgetting to call post_init() in a custom PreTrainedModel, which skips weight initialisation and other setup steps.

quiz.q: What do you need so that AutoModel.from_pretrained('tiny') loads your custom class?
options: Register the config's model_type with AutoConfig and map the config to the model with AutoModel.register
Save the model as a pickle
Nothing, Auto classes detect any nn.Module
quiz.explain: Auto classes dispatch on config.model_type, so both registrations are needed for local custom models.
